claim: The word function has many different meanings in molecular biology.
source: The word function has many different meanings in molecular biology.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary assertion of the paper.

claim: The analysis of function meanings is based on 20 abstracts from de novo gene birth research.
source: Based on an analysis of 20 abstracts we propose a simple lexicon that, we believe, will help scientists and philosophers discuss the meaning of function more clearly.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the sample size and methodology.

claim: The scientific enterprise is inherently rhetorical.
source: The scientific enterprise is inherently rhetorical (Condit, 1999; Fahnestock, 2002; Ceccarelli, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three scholarly works on the rhetoric of science.

claim: Language influences how we communicate, think, and practice science.
source: Language influences how we communicate, how we think, and how we practice science.
evidence: This is a general assertion about the role of language in science, drawing on established understanding in rhetoric and communication studies.

claim: Confusion and conflict can arise when the same word is understood differently by authors and readers.
source: In practice, however, confusion and even conflict can arise when the same word is understood differently by authors and readers.
evidence: This is presented as a general principle about scientific communication.

claim: A reader's interpretation of a word depends on factors including their field of training, country of origin, birth decade, and metaphysical presuppositions.
source: What is their field of training? In what country did they grow up? In what decade were they born? What are their metaphysical presuppositions? All these and countless other factors act as a filter between the words themselves and the meanings that readers assign to them.
evidence: This claim is based on general understanding of how context affects interpretation.

claim: The ENCODE Project debate about what fraction of the human genome is functional was prompted by different interpretations of the word 'functional'.
source: A striking example of different interpretations of words leading to controversy was the debate, prompted by the first papers from the ENCODE Project, about what fraction of the human genome is 'functional'. Is it approximately 80%, as suggested by biochemical evidence, or is it closer to 10%, as it appears from evolutionary evidence (The ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Doolittle, 2013; Graur et al., 2013; Kellis et al., 2014)?
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the ENCODE papers and subsequent debate papers.

claim: For most evolutionary biologists, function relates to selection (the effect for which the gene was selected in the past at the organismal level).
source: For most evolutionary biologists, function relates to selection (that is, the effect for which the gene was selected in the past at the organismal level).
evidence: This is presented as a characterization of how evolutionary biologists typically understand function.

claim: For most molecular geneticists and biochemists, function is generally associated with a molecule's activity (such as catalysis or binding), independent of historical factors.
source: For most molecular geneticists and biochemists, it is generally associated with a molecule's activity (such as catalysis or binding), independent of the historical factors that led to its existence.
evidence: This is presented as a characterization of how molecular geneticists and biochemists typically understand function.

claim: Some argue that the evolutionary meaning of function is the only one relevant for DNA sequences.
source: Yet some argue that the evolutionary meaning of function is the only one that is relevant for DNA sequences (Graur et al., 2013) and that when referring to other meanings scientists should use other words such as 'effect' or 'activity' (Doolittle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graur et al., 2013 and Doolittle et al., 2014.

claim: The debate about function echoes an ongoing conversation in the philosophy of science.
source: This position, and the arguments against it, echo an ongoing conversation in the philosophy of science (Cummins, 1975; Millikan, 1989; Neander, 1991; Amundson and Lauder, 1994; Garson, 2011; Griffiths, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple philosophical works.

claim: The philosophical conversation about function divides those who argue function should mean why an entity does what it does (selected effect definition) and those who argue it can also mean what an entity does (causal role definition).
source: In brief, the conversation divides those who argue function should mean why an entity does what it does (the selected effect definition of function) and those who argue it can also mean what an entity does (the causal role definition of function) (Laubichler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim summarizes philosophical positions and is supported by citation to Laubichler et al., 2015.

claim: Function strictly defined as selected effect is the historical explanation for the existence of an entity.
source: Function strictly defined as selected effect is the historical explanation for the existence of an entity (Millikan, 1989).
evidence: This claim defines a philosophical position and is supported by citation to Millikan, 1989.

claim: Function as causal role is ahistorical and describes the contribution of an entity to a complex system.
source: Function as causal role is ahistorical and describes the contribution of an entity to a complex system (Cummins, 1975).
evidence: This claim defines a philosophical position and is supported by citation to Cummins, 1975.

claim: Other theories of biological function have been proposed beyond selected effect and causal role perspectives.
source: Other theories of biological function have been proposed (Wouters, 2003; Mossio et al., 2009; Roux, 2014), but the selected effect/causal role perspectives have dominated the conversation in the context of genomics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to alternative theoretical frameworks.

claim: The selected effect/causal role perspectives have dominated the conversation about function in the context of genomics.
source: Other theories of biological function have been proposed (Wouters, 2003; Mossio et al., 2009; Roux, 2014), but the selected effect/causal role perspectives have dominated the conversation in the context of genomics.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment.

claim: The debate about function has sparked thoughtful studies that have advanced thinking at the interface of evolutionary biology and genomics.
source: Far from a fruitless dispute over semantics, the rhetorico-scientific debate has sparked a number of thoughtful studies that have advanced thinking at the interface of evolutionary biology and genomics.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent citations to specific studies.

claim: One study interrogates the relationship between organismal complexity and the number of functional elements in a genome.
source: For instance, one study interrogates the relationship between organismal complexity and the number of functional elements in a genome (Doolittle, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doolittle, 2013.

claim: One study highlights the discrepancies between different lines of evidence used to infer functionality of DNA loci.
source: another highlights the discrepancies between different lines of evidence used to infer functionality of DNA loci (Kellis et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kellis et al., 2014.

claim: One study refines the evolutionary classifications of genomic functions.
source: and another refines the evolutionary classifications of genomic functions (Graur et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Graur et al., 2015.

claim: Only a small fraction of biologists, mostly evolutionary biologists, are aware of the rhetorical context about function.
source: However, only a small fraction of biologists – mostly evolutionary biologists – are aware of the rhetorical context.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of awareness in the field.

claim: Most scientific publications do not explicitly include a definition of 'function' to clarify the meaning of reported findings.
source: Most scientific publications do not explicitly include a definition of 'function' to clarify the meaning of the reported findings.
evidence: This is an observation about scientific practice that will be supported by the subsequent analysis.

claim: In biological research there is a conflation between what is 'functional' and what 'matters'.
source: For better or worse, in biological research there is a conflation between what is 'functional' and what 'matters'.
evidence: This is an assertion about scientific practice and values.

claim: Only genomic sequences deemed 'functional' are worthy of being curated by reference databases, named, cloned, or incorporated into grant proposals for mechanistic studies.
source: Only those genomic sequences deemed 'functional' are worthy of being curated by reference databases, of being named, cloned or incorporated into grant proposals for mechanistic studies.
evidence: This is an observation about how the concept of function influences scientific practice.

claim: Scientists cannot agree on the number of functional genes in the human genome.
source: Today, scientists cannot agree on the number of functional genes in the human genome (Pertea et al., 2018; Jungreis et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two papers with presumably different estimates.

claim: Scientists cannot agree on what evidence should be required to elevate noncoding RNAs from mere transcriptional noise to functional regulatory elements.
source: or on what evidence should be required to elevate noncoding RNAs from mere transcriptional noise to functional regulatory elements (Doolittle, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doolittle, 2018.

claim: Some have pleaded for the community to deal with the 'F-word' urgently.
source: The general confusion about what exactly is meant by 'function' across the literature is such that some have pleaded for the community to deal with the 'F-word' urgently (Doolittle et al., 2014; Doolittle, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doolittle et al., 2014 and Doolittle, 2018.

claim: The field of de novo gene birth attempts to understand how new 'functional' genes can emerge without having derived from another gene as their ancestor.
source: This field attempts to understand how new 'functional' genes can emerge without having derived from another gene as their ancestor.
evidence: This is a description of the research focus of the de novo gene birth field.

claim: The process of de novo gene birth was long thought to be implausible on the basis that the probability that a functional protein would appear de novo by random association of amino acids is practically zero.
source: The process of de novo gene birth was long thought to be implausible on the basis that, as Francois Jacob wrote: "the probability that a functional protein would appear de novo by random association of amino acids is practically zero" (Jacob, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jacob, 1977.

claim: The explosion of new genome sequences has revealed that many genes have species- or lineage-specific sequences, suggesting they lack gene ancestors.
source: However, the explosion of new genome sequences has revealed that many genes have species- or lineage-specific sequences (Khalturin et al., 2009), suggesting that they lack gene ancestors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khalturin et al., 2009 and represents an inference from genomic data.

claim: Studies of a growing number of individual gene candidates have confirmed their de novo emergence.
source: Studies of a growing number of individual gene candidates have confirmed their de novo emergence, fueling many genomic and evolutionary studies to evaluate the scale and mechanisms of the de novo gene birth phenomenon (Tautz and Domazet-Lošo, 2011; McLysaght and Hurst, 2016; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review papers summarizing the field.

claim: The meanings of function are at the heart of what constitutes a de novo gene birth event.
source: The meanings of function are at the heart of what constitutes a de novo gene birth event.
evidence: This is a central thesis of the paper.

claim: For a genomic sequence to be labelled as a gene, it must by definition have a function.
source: For a genomic sequence to be labelled as a gene, it must by definition have a function; it must express a product that participates in cellular processes and affects phenotypes in a way that is being maintained by selection.
evidence: This is presented as a definitional requirement in the field.

claim: A gene must express a product that participates in cellular processes and affects phenotypes in a way that is being maintained by selection.
source: For a genomic sequence to be labelled as a gene, it must by definition have a function; it must express a product that participates in cellular processes and affects phenotypes in a way that is being maintained by selection.
evidence: This is presented as part of the definition of a gene.

claim: If a gene has evolved de novo, the locus it came from by definition was not a gene and did not have a function, or at least not a function of the same nature.
source: If such a gene has evolved de novo, the locus it came from by definition was not a gene, thus did not have a function, or at least not a function of the same nature as the one the new gene has.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of de novo gene birth.

claim: The molecular objects of study in de novo gene birth are transitioning between a state without a function and a state with a function.
source: The molecular objects of study are thus transitioning between a state without a function and a state with a function.
evidence: This is a characterization of the nature of de novo gene birth.

claim: De novo emerging sequences cannot have upon birth a function by the strict selected effect definition, since their existence cannot have been caused historically by past selection.
source: They cannot have upon birth a function by the strict selected effect definition (Millikan, 1989), since their existence cannot have been caused historically by a past selection.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the selected effect definition and is supported by citation to Millikan, 1989.

claim: The transformative nature of the de novo emergence process renders the debates about when and how a locus actually becomes functional highly contentious.
source: The transformative nature of the de novo emergence process thus renders the debates about when and how a locus actually becomes functional highly contentious.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of debate in the field.

claim: The de novo field is interdisciplinary and relatively young.
source: In addition to these fundamental considerations, the de novo field is interdisciplinary and relatively young.
evidence: This is a characterization of the field.

claim: The de novo field is rich in diverse perspectives and trainings.
source: It is therefore rich in diverse perspectives and trainings, and de novo researchers lack a commonly accepted jargon.
evidence: This is an inference from the interdisciplinary nature of the field.

claim: De novo researchers lack a commonly accepted jargon.
source: It is therefore rich in diverse perspectives and trainings, and de novo researchers lack a commonly accepted jargon.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field.

claim: De novo gene evolution is a well-suited test bed to evaluate what meanings of function are circulating in the field and whether the meanings of function hinder scientific communication.
source: All these challenges make de novo gene evolution a well-suited test bed to evaluate what meanings of function are circulating in this field and whether, and to what extent, the meanings of function hinder scientific communication.
evidence: This is a rationale for the study design.

claim: Authors writing about the function of a molecular object in the analyzed abstracts were almost always describing one or more of five properties: Expression, Capacities, Interactions, Physiological Implications and Evolutionary Implications.
source: Through an organized, iterative process of defining and discussing usages of the term, we inductively converged on the interpretation that, in this set of abstracts, authors writing about the function of a molecular object were almost always describing one or more of the following properties of the object: Expression, Capacities, Interactions, Physiological Implications and Evolutionary Implications.
evidence: This is a finding from the qualitative analysis of abstracts.

claim: The hierarchical order of the meanings in the Pittsburgh model was inspired from a reductionist interpretation of the flow of genetic information over time and space.
source: The hierarchical order of the meanings did not directly derive from our textual analysis, but was inspired from a reductionist interpretation of the flow of genetic information over time and space.
evidence: This is stated in the table caption and explains the theoretical basis for the model structure.

claim: The hierarchical order in the Pittsburgh model reflects a possible ordering of the series of properties that must be acquired by a locus to undergo de novo gene birth.
source: It also reflects a possible ordering of the series of properties that must be acquired by a locus to undergo de novo gene birth.
evidence: This is stated in the table caption and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Expression is not sufficient to cause Evolutionary Implications.
source: For instance, as has been discussed in the context of the ENCODE debate, Expression is not sufficient to cause Evolutionary Implications (Doolittle, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doolittle, 2018 and represents a logical relationship between the model components.

claim: Evolutionary Implications do not necessarily imply Expression since a locus can influence population dynamics through a DNA regulatory activity.
source: Inversely, Evolutionary Implications do not necessarily imply Expression since a locus can influence population dynamics through a DNA regulatory activity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationships between model components.

claim: The Pittsburgh model acknowledges epistemological relationships between different meanings of function while enabling researchers to describe them independently of each other.
source: Our model acknowledges epistemological relationships between different meanings of function while enabling researchers to describe them independently of each other.
evidence: This is a description of a feature of the proposed model.

claim: The Pittsburgh model presents practical advantages relative to pre-existing models because it is tailored to one field of research.
source: This model presents practical advantages relative to pre-existing ones because it is tailored to one field of research.
evidence: This is an assertion about the advantages of the proposed model.

claim: The Pittsburgh model differentiates between different types of biochemical activities for de novo emerging sequences.
source: In particular, it differentiates between different types of biochemical activities for de novo emerging sequences; this enables scientists to articulate more specific functional inferences than with broad terms that generalize across fields such as 'causal role' or 'mere activities' (Cummins, 1975; Wouters, 2003; Doolittle, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of a feature of the model, with citations to alternative approaches.

claim: The Pittsburgh model decomposes the complex concept of function into a hierarchical organization of measurable properties of the object in time and space according to meanings that are circulating in the field currently.
source: Rather than theorizing upon the legitimacy of what function should mean, our model decomposes this complex concept into a hierarchical organization of measurable properties of the object in time and space according to meanings that are circulating in the field currently.
evidence: This is a description of the approach taken in developing the model.

claim: The Pittsburgh model can be seen as a conceptual tool well adapted to describe molecular objects (DNA loci, RNA transcripts and proteins) in a manner that roughly maps to subfields of training and associated measurement techniques currently used in de novo gene birth research.
source: The Pittsburgh model of function can be seen as a conceptual tool well adapted to describe molecular objects (DNA loci, RNA transcripts and proteins) in a manner that roughly maps to subfields of training and associated measurement techniques currently used in de novo gene birth research.
evidence: This is a characterization of the intended use of the model.

claim: RNA-sequencing readily informs upon Expression.
source: For instance, while RNA-sequencing readily informs upon Expression and yeast two-hybrid upon Interactions
evidence: This is based on knowledge of what RNA-sequencing measures.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid readily informs upon Interactions.
source: For instance, while RNA-sequencing readily informs upon Expression and yeast two-hybrid upon Interactions
evidence: This is based on knowledge of what yeast two-hybrid assays measure.

claim: Discovering interactions by yeast two-hybrid does not allow the researcher to conclude that a locus is natively expressed.
source: discovering interactions by yeast two-hybrid does not allow the researcher to conclude that a locus is natively expressed
evidence: This is based on understanding of the limitations of yeast two-hybrid methodology.

claim: Establishing that a locus is expressed does not imply that the corresponding product necessarily interacts with other elements in the cell.
source: so too, establishing that a locus is expressed does not imply that the corresponding product necessarily interacts with other elements in the cell.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between expression and interaction.

claim: Neither RNA-sequencing nor yeast two-hybrid gives direct insights into Evolutionary Implications.
source: Evidently, neither technique gives direct insights into Evolutionary Implications since Expression and Interactions are necessary but not sufficient to cause Physiological Implications, let alone Evolutionary Implications.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of these techniques.

claim: Expression and Interactions are necessary but not sufficient to cause Physiological Implications.
source: Evidently, neither technique gives direct insights into Evolutionary Implications since Expression and Interactions are necessary but not sufficient to cause Physiological Implications, let alone Evolutionary Implications.
evidence: This is a logical claim about the relationships between the model components.

claim: Separating the five meanings from one another enables communicating with increased precision about what the findings are.
source: Separating these meanings from one another enables communicating with increased precision about what the findings are, thereby helping to fallacious logical shortcuts such as 'this protein is expressed therefore it is functional therefore it is under selection'.
evidence: This is an assertion about the benefit of the proposed model.

claim: The meanings of Physiological Implications and Evolutionary Implications are deliberately broad to allow for detailed descriptions beyond the somewhat restrictive notion of selected effect.
source: The meanings of Physiological Implications and Evolutionary Implications are deliberately broad to allow for detailed descriptions beyond the somewhat restrictive notion of selected effect.
evidence: This is a description of a design choice in the model.

claim: Evolutionary Implications can refer to selection upon a trait driven by the object in the past, as in the strict definition of selected effect.
source: For instance, Evolutionary Implications can refer to selection upon a trait driven by the object in the past, as in the strict definition of selected effect (Millikan, 1989), but it can equally describe other ways the object may influence population dynamics such as runaway selection or novel fitness enhancing effects.
evidence: This is a description of what the Evolutionary Implications category can encompass, with citation to Millikan, 1989.

claim: Evolutionary Implications can describe other ways the object may influence population dynamics such as runaway selection or novel fitness enhancing effects.
source: For instance, Evolutionary Implications can refer to selection upon a trait driven by the object in the past, as in the strict definition of selected effect (Millikan, 1989), but it can equally describe other ways the object may influence population dynamics such as runaway selection or novel fitness enhancing effects.
evidence: This is a description of what the Evolutionary Implications category can encompass.

claim: The Pittsburgh model was tested on only 20 abstracts related to the single field of de novo gene birth.
source: Tested on only 20 abstracts related to the single field of de novo gene birth, by no means does it represent a complete ontology of function.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: The Pittsburgh model does not represent a complete ontology of function.
source: Tested on only 20 abstracts related to the single field of de novo gene birth, by no means does it represent a complete ontology of function.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the model's limitations.

claim: The Pittsburgh model may or may not extend to genomic elements outside of the gene birth framework, such as selfish elements or promoters.
source: Constructed in a field-specific manner, our model may or may not extend to genomic elements outside of the gene birth framework, such as selfish elements or promoters.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the model's generalizability.

claim: The Pittsburgh model cannot be readily applied to biological objects other than DNA, RNA and protein objects.
source: It cannot be readily applied to biological objects other than DNA, RNA and protein objects.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the model's applicability.

claim: There may be additional meanings of function available beyond the five included in the Pittsburgh model.
source: There may be additional meanings available beyond the five we included, and different ways to characterize the relationships between these meanings.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential limitations of the model.

claim: The abstracts analyzed generally provided enough context for each independent reader to confidently assign meanings to most instances.
source: The abstracts generally provided enough context for each independent reader to confidently assign meanings to most instances, with only rare assignments of the label 'vague' (9 instances with one or more vague assignment, none unanimous).
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative analysis with specific numbers provided.

claim: Only 9 instances had one or more vague assignment, and none were unanimously assigned as vague.
source: The abstracts generally provided enough context for each independent reader to confidently assign meanings to most instances, with only rare assignments of the label 'vague' (9 instances with one or more vague assignment, none unanimous).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the data analysis.

claim: The Pittsburgh model gave readers a key to decipher more specifically what authors meant by the word function.
source: Hence, the Pittsburgh model gave readers a key to decipher more specifically what authors meant by the word function.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that readers could assign meanings.

claim: Only 12% (5/42) of assignments were unanimous, where the same single meaning was chosen by all readers.
source: However, and importantly, a quantitative analysis revealed only that 12% (5/42) of assignments were unanimous, where the same single meaning was chosen by all readers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 88% (37/42) of instances of the word function in the same sentence were interpreted differently by team members.
source: In other words, the same instance of the word in the same sentence was most of the times (37/42 = 88%) interpreted differently by our team members.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: The most confusing instances, with 4 or 6 distinct assignments, were all assigned 'vague' by at least one reader.
source: The most confusing instances, with 4 or 6 distinct assignments, were all assigned 'vague' by at least one reader.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the data.

claim: When the meaning of function is unspecified, the literature in the field of de novo gene birth can become confusing.
source: This analysis indicates that when the meaning of function is unspecified, the literature in this field of research can become confusing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis.

claim: Consensus was successfully reached for all but one instance of function usage.
source: Consensus was successfully reached for all but one instance, suggesting that the Pittsburgh model enabled adequate description of most of the instances of function in our abstract database.
evidence: This is a finding from the consensus-building process.

claim: The Pittsburgh model enabled adequate description of most of the instances of function in the abstract database.
source: Consensus was successfully reached for all but one instance, suggesting that the Pittsburgh model enabled adequate description of most of the instances of function in our abstract database.
evidence: This is an inference from the successful consensus-building.

claim: The fraction of instances assigned a unique meaning grew from 5/42 (12%) in independent assignments to 26/42 (62%) in consensus assignments.
source: We then quantified again the fraction of instances of function that were assigned a unique meaning. This number grew from 5/42 (12%) in the original independent assignments (Figure 1A) to 26/42 (62%) in the consensus assignments (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding comparing independent and consensus assignments, shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: 50% (21/42) of instances were interpreted differently by at least one of four readers upon independent reading of the texts.
source: This shows that, in our analyses, 21/42 (50%) instances were interpreted differently by at least one of four readers upon independent reading of the texts.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: After establishing consensus assignments, 16/42 (38%) instances were assigned two or three meanings.
source: It is notable that, after establishing consensus assignments, still 16/42 (38%) instances were assigned two or three meanings (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the consensus analysis, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The word function is often used to mean different things, and the plurality of function cannot be easily disentangled.
source: This suggests that this one word is often used to mean different things, and that the plurality of function cannot be easily disentangled.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that many instances were assigned multiple meanings even after consensus.

claim: The meanings most frequently found in consensus assignments were Physiological Implications (21 instances) and Evolutionary Implications (18 instances).
source: The meanings most frequently found in our consensus assignments were Physiological Implications (21 instances) and Evolutionary Implications (18 instances; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the consensus analysis, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Physiological Implications and Evolutionary Implications were most often found assigned together in cases where a single instance was assigned two or three meanings (6 instances).
source: These two were also most often found assigned together in cases where a single instance was assigned two or three meanings (6 instances).
evidence: This is a specific finding about co-occurrence of meanings.

claim: All but one instances with a vague consensus assignment were nouns.
source: Interestingly though, all but one instances with a vague consensus assignment were nouns.
evidence: This is a specific finding about the relationship between part of speech and vagueness.

claim: The use of function in the de novo gene birth field is hard to interpret.
source: Yet our rhetorical approach leads us to conclude that the use of function in this field is hard to interpret, and that further nuance in writing would assist the reader in understanding how the authors intend their results to be interpreted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall analysis.

claim: Further nuance in writing would assist the reader in understanding how the authors intend their results to be interpreted.
source: Yet our rhetorical approach leads us to conclude that the use of function in this field is hard to interpret, and that further nuance in writing would assist the reader in understanding how the authors intend their results to be interpreted.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: The word function carries convoluted meanings that complicate the scientific conversation.
source: In summary, our results provide quantitative support to previous assertions (Doolittle, 2018; Laubichler et al., 2015) that the word function carries convoluted meanings that complicate the scientific conversation.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the quantitative analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: Function becomes an ambiguous concept when applied to the edge case of de novo gene birth, which can lead to confusion in interpretation of the literature.
source: Our rhetorical analysis shows that function becomes an ambiguous concept when applied to the edge case of de novo gene birth, which can lead to confusion in interpretation of the literature.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the rhetorical analysis.

claim: Scientific communication is hindered by the use of the word function within the de novo gene birth field.
source: Whether multiple meanings are intended by the authors, or meanings unintended by the authors are interpreted by the readers, or a combination of both, the fact is that scientific communication is hindered by the use of this word within the de novo gene birth field.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the overall analysis.

claim: The cultural diversity of readers in the de novo gene birth field effectively prevents a unique definition of function to be imposed in practice.
source: There may be excellent theoretical arguments to be made about why function should mean one thing or another, but the cultural diversity of readers in this emerging field effectively prevents a unique definition to be imposed in practice.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of diversity in the field.

claim: It will be productive for scientists to acknowledge the diversity of onto-epistemological perspectives in the de novo gene birth field and adapt their writing style accordingly.
source: We believe that it will be productive for scientists to acknowledge the diversity of onto-epistemological perspectives in this field and adapt their writing style accordingly.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: The authors endorse qualifying the use of function or avoiding the word altogether.
source: Rather than privileging one meaning of function over another, we endorse qualifying the use of function or avoiding the word altogether (Doolittle, 2018).
evidence: This is a recommendation with citation to Doolittle, 2018.

claim: The Pittsburgh model will provide a useful tool for scientists to contextualize their writing so the relationship between observations and functional inferences can be clarified.
source: We hope our model will provide a useful tool for scientists to contextualize their writing so the relationship between the observations reported and the functional inferences made can be clarified and the risk of misunderstanding can be reduced.
evidence: This is a statement of the intended utility of the model.

claim: Function is a concept that depends on the methodological practices, measurement procedures and habits of scientists.
source: Function is a concept that depends on the methodological practices, measurement procedures and habits of scientists.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about the nature of the concept of function.

claim: As methodological practices, measurement procedures and habits of scientists change, the concept of function will change and adapt to specific subfields of research.
source: As these change, so too will the concept of function change and adapt to specific subfields of research, because it is contingent and always in a state of flux.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about how the concept of function evolves.

claim: Function requires ongoing attention and theorizing by the scientific community.
source: Function requires ongoing attention and theorizing by the scientific community.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: The Pittsburgh model is expected to develop and adapt with scientific practice.
source: Therefore, we expect our model to develop and adapt with scientific practice.
evidence: This is a prediction about the future evolution of the model.

claim: The authors encourage researchers to refine the Pittsburgh model, adapt it to other subfields of genomics and other types of biological objects, and propose alternatives.
source: We encourage researchers to refine the model, adapt it to other subfields of genomics and other types of biological objects (metabolites, cell types, organs), and propose alternatives.
evidence: This is a call to action for future research.

claim: Computational natural language processing could be used to generate field-specific models by automatic analysis of large bodies of literature.
source: One can envision, for instance, exploiting the power of computational natural language processing to generate field-specific models by automatic analysis of large bodies of literature (Friedman et al., 2001; Groth et al., 2016), perhaps using our modest manual analysis as a training set.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work with citations to relevant methods.

claim: The authors hope that interdisciplinary conversations about philosophy, rhetoric and scientific concepts will accompany the emergence of new scientific fields in the future.
source: More generally, we hope that interdisciplinary conversations about philosophy (Laplane et al., 2019), rhetoric and scientific concepts will accompany the emergence of new scientific fields in the future.
